name: Corset training (tightlacing)

lead: Corset training means wearing a corset laced more tightly over time to slim the waist and exaggerate the hourglass shape. Wearers and corset makers describe an immediate smoothing and cinching effect, and some report that the waist stays smaller for a time after the corset is removed.

It has a long history, with tightlacing peaking in 19th-century Europe and America, and it survives today in historical reenactment, alternative fashion and waist-training communities. Doctors since the 1800s have written about its effects on breathing and the body.

paras: Practitioners describe starting with a well-fitted, steel-boned corset and wearing it for longer periods as the body adapts, then gradually lacing tighter. Modern waist trainers are elasticated garments marketed with similar aims, though less rigid than corsets.

Wikipedia's corset article reports reduced lung capacity (average about 9% in moderate lacing), breathlessness, shallow breathing and discomfort once reduction passes a few inches. Long use is linked to core and back muscle weakening, and historical physicians reported fainting, digestive trouble and pelvic effects. People with respiratory, digestive or spinal conditions are usually advised by clinicians to avoid it.

angle.text: A laced corset narrows the waist visibly and creates an hourglass silhouette immediately. Practitioners train by wearing it longer and tighter over time, hoping to carry some reduction beyond wear.

lead: Tightlacing, also called corset training, is the practice of wearing an increasingly tight corset to reshape the waist and posture.[1][2] The aim is a smaller waist and a pronounced hourglass figure, which wearers achieve visually while the corset is worn and, according to practitioners, can retain to a degree.[3]

Corsets were standard Western underwear for about four centuries, but tightlacing rose in the late 1820s and 1830s after metal eyelets were introduced in 1827, which allowed much tighter lacing.[1][2] Historian David Kunzle estimated that average corseted waists in the 1880s were about 21 inches, with typical reductions of 2 to 6 inches.[1][2] Corsets declined in the 1910s and 1920s and later survived in fetish, alternative and goth fashion and among historical reenactors.[1][2]

Physicians and dress reformers criticised tightlacing from the nineteenth century, and medical journals of the period carry numerous articles on its effects.[4][5][6][7] Modern accounts describe measurable reductions in lung capacity and comfort during moderate lacing.

paras: Tightlacing differs from ordinary corset wear, which mostly supported the bust and posture and was laced to a comfortable degree.[3] Modern waist training uses milder, often elasticated garments for intermittent wear, whereas tightlacing emphasises near-constant, strong constriction, according to Grokipedia.[3]

Stays and corsets appear in Renaissance Europe, and steel boning had become popular by 1850.[1][3] The spoon busk, developed in the 1870s, shaped the stomach.[1] Training sometimes began in childhood or adolescence, with girls given progressively smaller corsets; corsets became widely available through mass manufacturing.[2]

In 1998 Guinness changed its category to smallest waist on a living person; Cathie Jung held it at 15 inches after Ethel Granger's 13-inch record.[1][2] Others recorded with very small waists include Empress Elisabeth of Austria at 16 inches.[2]

Moderate lacing reduced lung capacity by 2 to 29 percent, about 9 percent on average, in research summarised by Wikipedia, and a reenactor study found comfort significantly affected beyond about 3 inches of reduction.[1] Long-term use may weaken core and back muscles.[1][3]

Nineteenth-century physicians described morbid effects and the results of tightlacing, including fainting and displaced organs.[4][5][6][7] A 1901 article linked tightlacing to nephroptosis.[8] Historians note that claims of rib removal for small waists are not supported, and Wikipedia notes harm was not systematically documented in period sources despite strong claims by critics.[1][2] Skeletal studies indicate that sustained corseting from youth can change ribs and spine.[1][9]

Corset training is discussed mainly in fashion and body-modification communities rather than as a core looksmaxxing topic. Proponents describe it as a way to achieve and maintain a dramatic waist, while clinicians and historians emphasise the physical costs.

No studies found. Modern controlled research on tightlacing is limited; the evidence consists of historical medical writings, bioarchaeology such as a 2012 paleopathology paper on binding practices, and small studies of corset wear.[9][1]
